d.s: The first object known to come from another star was oddly shaped, tumbled, and accelerated slightly more than gravity explains. One astronomer argued it was a light sail. The argument is interesting and the evidence is thin.
A short video of a masked figure with coded imagery, mailed on a DVD and posted online. The codes have been partly decoded; the purpose has not.
Consumer DNA databases used to identify criminal suspects through their relatives. The practice is documented and consequential.
A claim that mobile networks caused or spread the disease. It led to attacks on masts and to real harm.

d.t: A White Dwarf as a Weapon
d.s: The claim that a stellar remnant could be steered, or used, as a weapon. It appears in science fiction and in UFO lore; the physics of moving a star is the objection.
Oil is not made from fossils in the way schoolbooks imply — but it is organic. The claim that it forms abiotically in the mantle has been tested for a century and has produced no commercial field.
A theory that the family matriarch is the film's antagonist. It is an interpretation of a work of animation.
The claim that sound could have lifted the stones of ancient monuments. Acoustic levitation is real, and it works on objects the size of a grain of rice.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Some of the people who build these systems put a double-digit probability on them causing catastrophe. Others with equal expertise put it near zero. Both are reasoning from the same absence of evidence.
One pharaoh replaced Egypt's gods with a single sun disc, moved the capital, and changed the art. The revolution is documented; why it happened is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A book of machines — clocks, water-raising devices and automata — with drawings clear enough to rebuild. The book survives.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Heavy drinking damages the brain. The mechanism is not the death of cells in the way the phrase suggests.
Did Alexander the Great die of disease or poison? The sources disagree and the body is lost.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Alexander the Great died in Babylon and his body was taken to Egypt. His tomb was visited for centuries, and it has never been found.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: In 2016 three papers proved, within months of each other, that several intuitive definitions of fairness cannot hold together. The field has been arguing about what to do with that ever since.
The claim that recommendation systems push people toward extremes. The mechanism is plausible, the evidence is thinner than the headlines, and the platform data that would settle it is not available.
A hand that acts on its own — unbuttoning a shirt, grabbing a tool, resisting the other hand — is a real consequence of damage to the connections between the hemispheres.
The United States government spent twenty-two years investigating flying saucers, catalogued 12,618 sightings, and left 701 unexplained. That is a real number, and it means less than it sounds.
The leading theory of Alzheimer's produced drugs that mostly failed, then two that worked slightly. That combination is more informative than either a vindication or a debunking.
The Atlantic overturning circulation may weaken or collapse. The physics is documented; the timing and likelihood are argued.
The Gulf Stream is not a conveyor belt that can simply switch off, but the Atlantic overturning that carries heat north is weakening. How far, how fast, and whether it collapses is unsettled.
The amyloid cascade hypothesis has driven thirty years of Alzheimer's research. Two drugs now remove amyloid and slow decline slightly; whether that vindicates the hypothesis is still argued.
The theory is not that ancient people were stupid. It is that they were clever enough to describe spacecraft, and that archaeologists have been reading the descriptions wrong.
A story about a man who turned $800 into $350 million and claimed to be a time traveller. It ran in a supermarket tabloid.
A theory that the game is set after humanity. It is a reading of a fiction, and the game is cheerful.
The joke theory that the game's cheerful village is a coercive community. It is a reading of the game's mechanics, and the game's designers did not intend it.
Some people close their eyes and see nothing. The condition was described in 1880, named in 2015, and is now the best-studied example of how differently ordinary minds are furnished.
Mirrors on the walls of Syracuse, focusing sunlight onto Roman ships. The story is late, the physics is marginal, and the experiments have produced smoke and no fire.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: Aristarchus Put the Sun at the Centre
d.s: A Greek astronomer proposed a heliocentric system eighteen centuries before Copernicus. The report survives, and the idea was rejected.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A seven-time winner stripped of his titles after a doping investigation and a confession.
The earliest mention of Arthur is a battle list written three centuries after he supposedly lived. The claim that he was a Roman officer is a modern attempt to fill the gap.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Both asbestos and radon were known hazards long before they were regulated, and in both cases industry documents show the knowledge preceded the action.
A dating site whose user base included large numbers of fabricated female profiles. The data leak made it measurable.
A YouTube channel presented as a missing person's video diary. It is fiction, and it was built to be mistaken for real.
A sweetener classified as possibly carcinogenic, and the dose that matters.

A proposed measure of how complex an object is, by counting the minimum steps needed to build it. Its authors argue it explains selection and can detect life; its critics argue it measures construction, not causation.
The Minoan eruption of Santorini destroyed a civilisation, and the parallel with Plato's story is striking. The date is the problem: it is 9,000 years out.
A team argued that Atlantis lies under the marshes of Doñana in southern Spain, destroyed by a tsunami. The site has structures, and the identification is not accepted.
The claim that Atlantis was Antarctica, shifted to the pole by a crustal displacement. Plate tectonics does not permit it, and the ice cores are older than the claim requires.
A theory that the story repeats in a loop, with the protagonist trying again. The show's own time mechanics are strange enough to invite it.
A claim that the singer died in 2003 and was replaced by a body double named Melissa. The evidence is photographs, and the photographs are of the same person at different ages.
The ancestral homeland of the Mexica, described in colonial sources and located nowhere.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that the Mexica homeland was in Utah. The tradition is real; the location is not.

The Roman temple platform at Baalbek contains three stones of about 800 tonnes each. They were quarried, moved and set by Roman engineers, and the claim that only giants could have done it is an argument from incredulity with a documented answer.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The Tower of Babel is a story about language. A modern reading makes it a rocket launch facility, which requires ignoring what the text says and what Babylon actually built.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A clay tablet of Pythagorean triples, interpreted in 2017 as the world's oldest trigonometric table.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that rock records contain hidden messages played backwards. The messages are found by the listener, not put there.

Glowing spheres that drift through rooms during thunderstorms have been reported for four centuries, filmed once, and measured spectroscopically in a handful of cases. The reports are too consistent to dismiss and too rare to pin down.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: A reading of a film through a phrase from an unrelated film. It is an interpretation, not a claim.
Apple slowed down older iPhones to stop them shutting down unexpectedly, and did not tell anyone. It was a reasonable engineering decision and a serious communication failure.
A bank grew into a global institution by serving dictators, arms dealers and intelligence services, and was closed by regulators in 1991. It is the largest bank fraud prosecuted to that date.
If aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ with exponents above two, the three bases share a prime factor. There is a million-dollar prize and no proof.
A land bridge between Asia and America, exposed when sea levels fell. It was not just a corridor: people lived on it for thousands of years.
If the world continues past Antarctica, the continent is not a continent but a boundary — and the treaty that governs it becomes a cover story.
An annual off-the-record meeting of politicians, bankers and executives. It is real, it is influential, and it is not secret — the participant list is published every year.
A conjecture connecting the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to a function attached to it. It is the Millennium problem with the most computational support.
The white paper proposed a peer-to-peer electronic cash system. Fifteen years later its main use is as an asset whose price is quoted in the currency it was meant to replace.
A theory that every Black Mirror episode shares a universe, connected by background details. The details are real; the continuity is not.
Nobody predicted 2008, the pandemic or the smartphone. The interesting question is not that surprises happen but whether our models are built to be surprised by them.
Does time pass, or is the universe a four-dimensional block in which all moments exist? Physics constrains the answer without settling it.
The standard treatment for almost everything, practised for two thousand years, and harmful.

Short-wavelength light suppresses melatonin and shifts the body clock. That much is solid. The claim that screens damage the retina, or that blue-blocking glasses fix sleep, is where the evidence thins out.
A software system designed to correct a handling characteristic, fed by a single sensor, brought down two aircraft. 346 people died.
A theory that the horse died in a swimming pool and the rest of the series is his dying imagination. It is a reading of a show about a character who nearly dies.

If the universe fluctuates forever, a random self-aware brain with false memories is far more likely than an entire ordered cosmos. Nobody thinks that means you are one. It means something is wrong with the model.
Games said to make you smarter. You get better at the games.
The claim that brain-computer interfaces will merge people into a collective intelligence. The interfaces are real; the hive is not.
The energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude greater than the energy needed to produce it. It is the reason this archive exists in the form it does.

d.t: Breaking Bad and The Walking Dead
d.s: A theory that the two shows share a universe, built on a bag of blue meth and a timeline. It is a joke that got elaborate.
A claim that a celebrity's social media posts contain hidden messages. The reading is a community's, and the code is not established.
An essay in The Atlantic in 1982 argued that untended disorder invites serious crime. It became the operating theory of American policing, and then it was tested.
David Graeber's claim that a large share of jobs are pointless and their holders know it. The essay struck a nerve; the survey evidence is thinner than the argument.
A cave in Illinois said to hold thousands of inscribed stones from lost civilisations. The cave has never been shown to anyone.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, abandoned within two centuries. Its population and its end are both argued.
The emperor was said to have made his horse a consul. The sources are hostile, and the story is probably a joke about a private plan.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A political consulting firm obtained Facebook data on millions of users through a personality quiz app, and used it for targeted advertising. The scandal changed how the platform handled data.
Cancer is not one disease but a process: cells evolving inside a body, escaping the controls that make multicellular life possible. That framing explains more than any single cause does.
The idea that a story's fixed events must happen, used in a film and discussed as a rule of fiction.
A drowned kingdom under Cardigan Bay, kept out by a gate that was left open. The legend is real; the kingdom is not.
Mark Fisher's argument that capitalism has become the horizon of thought, so that alternatives are unimaginable. It is a diagnosis, not a measurement.
A claim that the Carnac stones were arranged to record earthquakes. The rows are real; the function is invented.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A Pixar shared-universe theory in which the cars inherited a world the humans left. It is a joke, and the films do not say it.
The idea that venting anger relieves it. The evidence says the opposite: rehearsal makes anger more accessible, and the studies that tested it found venting increases aggression.
Cattle found dead with clean cuts and missing organs, said to be the work of something unusual. The forensic explanations are ordinary and varied.
Photographs said to show famous people as vampires. They are digital composites made to look like old photographs.
Hundreds of kilometres of roads radiating from Chaco Canyon, built straight and often ending nowhere.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A culture that plated copper with gold using electrochemical methods, or so the claim goes. The objects are real; the method is argued.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The stone carvings at Chavín de Huántar show fanged deities, serpents and transformations. The visionary imagery is real, and the argument that the site's rituals used hallucinogens is supported by archaeological finds.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that aircraft are spraying chemicals to control populations or climate. The trails are ice crystals, they behave exactly as contrail physics predicts, and no sampling has found the chemicals.
A reactor that became unstable at low power, operated outside its limits, with a test that went wrong.
Swallowed gum passes through in days. The seven-year figure is folklore.
Gunpowder was formulated in China for medicine and fireworks, and by the Song dynasty it was a weapon.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A cat that appeared in hundreds of forum images, posted by a user who later explained the story.
Some patients have persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease. Whether that is an ongoing infection is the argument, and the trials have not supported prolonged antibiotics.
Glance at a clock and the first second seems to last longer. The clock is fine; your brain is filling a gap it never recorded.
The CIA ran a network of secret prisons in several countries, where detainees were held and subjected to techniques the US government later acknowledged as torture.
A temple site west of Alexandria has produced coins and a tunnel, and a claim that it holds Cleopatra's tomb. The excavator believes it; most Egyptologists are cautious.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The story that Cleopatra dissolved a pearl in vinegar to win a bet. The chemistry is doubtful and the source is late.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A short animation remembered by a viewer and identified years later. It is a lost-media success, and the memory turned out to be accurate.
Clouds both warm and cool the planet, and how they will change is the largest single uncertainty in climate projection. The sign is agreed; the size is not.
In Inception, Cobb spins a top to test reality — but the top was Mal's, not his. His actual totem is his wedding ring, which appears only in dreams.

Two electrochemists announced tabletop fusion on 23 March 1989. Within six months the effect had failed to replicate, and thirty-seven years later there is still a conference, a journal and no accepted mechanism.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: Durkheim's term for what happens when a crowd assembles and feels something together. It is not mysticism; it is the mechanism by which rituals make beliefs feel true.
The claim that groups have a measurable general intelligence, predicting performance across tasks. The original study was striking; the replications are mixed.

Penrose's proposal that the universe repeats, with each aeon's end becoming the next one's beginning. It makes a specific prediction about the microwave background, and the searches for it have not found it.
Whether a system can be conscious is not a question anyone can currently answer, and that is the finding: the tests measure behaviour, and behaviour is compatible with no inner life at all.
The proposal that the constants of nature may vary over cosmic time. Measurements keep finding no change, to extraordinary precision.
David Deutsch's proposal to rebuild physics around which transformations are possible, rather than around initial conditions.
One man carved and moved over a thousand tonnes of coral rock alone, at night, and refused to say how. The answer is levers, pulleys and patience.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: General relativity allows singularities with no event horizon — naked points where physics stops and the universe can be seen to break. Penrose conjectured they cannot form. Nobody has proved it.
A doctor cracked the knuckles of one hand for sixty years. The other hand was the control.

d.t: Creationism and the Alternatives to Darwin
d.l: Settled on descent, open on mechanism
d.s: Common ancestry is about as well supported as anything in science. How evolution works in detail is still argued about — by biologists. This page separates the two, claim by claim, without pretending the argument is even.
Cryptozoology has one legitimate test — produce the animal — and one recurring problem: the most famous photograph in the field was confessed to be a toy submarine.
A Swiss company sold encryption machines to governments around the world for decades. The CIA and the German BND owned it, and the machines were compromised by design.
The fastest way to get the right answer online is to post the wrong one. It is a joke about correction culture, and it is accurate often enough to be useful.
One curse has been checked with epidemiology, one was dismantled in a courtroom, and one was invented by a newspaper in 1908. All three are still going.
A man hijacked a passenger jet, took $200,000, and jumped into the night over the Pacific Northwest. He was never found, and the case is the only unsolved hijacking in US history.
Blades with a watery pattern, made from crucible steel imported from India, and famous for sharpness. The technique was lost in the eighteenth century, and the nanoscale explanation is contested.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Organisations run by code and token votes rather than managers. They exist, they hold real money, and their governance has produced both experiments and failures.

A 2008 analysis reported that galaxy clusters are all drifting toward a patch of sky beyond the observable universe. If true it would break the assumption that the universe looks the same in every direction. Later data did not confirm it.
The case that something invisible holds galaxies together is overwhelming. The case for any particular particle is not — and that gap is where the field currently lives.
A hypothetical particle that would interact weakly with ordinary matter, proposed as a bridge to a dark sector.
A fan theory that Jar Jar Binks was secretly a Sith lord, whose clownish behaviour was a cover. It is inventive, it is argued from staging and dialogue, and its authors know it is fiction.
The claim that dating apps score users and show them only to people of similar scores. One app did use an Elo-style system, and said it stopped.
Bringing back the mammoth, the thylacine or the passenger pigeon. The genetics is progressing, the ecology is harder, and no de-extincted animal exists yet.
A Soviet system designed to launch retaliation if the command authority were destroyed — a doomsday machine that actually exists, and is semi-automatic rather than automatic.
Nostalgia for places and times the person never knew, spread through images of empty shopping centres.
The character talks to the reader. The convention is documented; the 'proof' it gives about the character's world is not.
A Twitter thread about a ghost in an apartment, told in real time with drawings and photographs. It was a performance, and it was very good.
Ninety per cent of the web is “deep” in the most boring possible sense: it is behind a login, a paywall, or a search box. The dark web is a small encrypted subset of that, and it is not a place.
A well blowout that killed eleven people and spilled millions of barrels. The cement job and the decisions around it are documented.
Kant predicted it in 1795. Statistical work from the 1960s found it. Democracies fight plenty of wars — just not, on the whole, each other — and the explanation matters enormously for policy.
A Greek philosopher argued that matter consists of indivisible particles. He had no evidence, and he was right.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A hominin known from a finger bone, whose genes are in living people from Tibet to Melanesia.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: An underground city in Cappadocia with rooms, stables, a church and ventilation shafts, deep enough for thousands of people.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Patches that turn brown overnight and are said to draw out toxins. The colour is oxidation.
The most famous survivor story of the twentieth century, sustained by a woman who may have believed it herself, and ended by a blood sample taken from a British prince.
A U-boat to Argentina, a Nazi compound in Patagonia, a death staged in the bunker. The story has books, documentaries and declassified FBI files. It does not have a body that matches.
A supposed Nazi secret weapon called 'the Bell': a bell-shaped device said to use exotic physics. It appears in a 2000 book, and there is no contemporary document.
Volkswagen fitted cars with software that detected emissions tests and switched on full pollution control only when being tested. On the road, the cars emitted many times the limit.
A boulder covered in carvings, attributed to Phoenicians, Norse, Portuguese and Indigenous peoples.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that cities will be policed through real-time simulations of their populations. The components exist; the system does not.
Were the dinosaurs warm-blooded? Bone growth, isotopes and the nasal anatomy point in different directions, and the answer may be neither.
A landmass in the southern North Sea, drowned between about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago. Trawlers have brought up bones and tools for a century.
Clay figurines from Jōmon Japan have goggle-like eyes and patterned bodies. They were read as space suits. They are stylised figures, mostly female, and many were deliberately broken.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Domesticated animals share a set of traits — floppy ears, patchy coats, smaller brains — and the explanation is argued.
A theory that the cartoon villain is the boys' father. It is an interpretation, and the show has not confirmed it.
Every culture on Earth independently invented a giant reptile. In 2013, a team tried to work out whether they did it independently at all.
The suggestion that dragon myths around the world grew from fossil bones. The bones are everywhere; the stories differ.
The Sun has no companion today. That is a measurement, not an opinion — and yet the “second sun” idea is one of the most persistent in fringe cosmology, because it is half right.
Dunbar plotted neocortex size against group size across primates and extrapolated to humans: about 150 stable relationships. Armies, firms and villages seemed to fit. Then the statistics were redone.
Frank Herbert wrote Dune as a warning about charismatic leaders and the danger of following them. The films and the fandom have often read it as a hero story.
Low performers overestimate their ability. The effect is real and the popular version — a graph with a peak of confidence on a mountain of stupidity — is not what the paper showed.
Ruins have been found under the sea off Gujarat, and they are real. The claim that they are the 32,000-year-old city of Krishna is not supported by their dating.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Nine experienced ski hikers cut their way out of a tent in the night and died in the snow. Sixty years later, two physicists modelled the snow and closed most of the gap.

A civilisation that captured all its star's light would be visible from far away, as an excess of infrared and a deficit of visible light. Astronomers have looked, and found candidates that turned out to be dust.
A solid shell around a star is gravitationally impossible. A swarm of collectors is not, and the difference matters: the swarm is the version astronomers actually search for.
The sense that this moment was dreamed before. It is distinct from déjà vu, it is common, and the tempting explanation — that the dream predicted the event — is the one the evidence does not support.
The feeling that this has happened before, with no memory of when. Most people have it, nobody has a settled explanation, and the one thing it is not is evidence of a previous life.
A cameo put E.T.'s species in the Star Wars senate, and a fan theory built a shared universe on it. The cameo is real; the universe is a joke.

The claim that Earth was engineered for life — by an earlier civilisation, or by design. It borrows the language of a real scientific debate about fine-tuning and rare Earth, and then adds an agent nobody has evidence for.
Nobody can say where and when a large earthquake will happen. A great deal of money and a long list of methods have gone into trying, and the failures are more instructive than the successes.

The theory is intuitive: recommendation systems show you what you already agree with, and you drift outward. The experiments that changed people's feeds found the drift was smaller than expected — and not always in the predicted direction.
A claim that the Genesis garden can be located by its rivers. The text names four rivers; two cannot be identified.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that the Garden of Eden was in Missouri, with a stone altar to prove it. The stone is real; the garden is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Dietary cholesterol was said to raise blood cholesterol and heart risk. The advice has been revised, and the debate continues.
For fifteen years, 'willpower is a finite resource like a battery' was textbook psychology, complete with the advice to drink sugar water. Then the replications came back near zero.
A theory that a planet-sized character's memories are fabrications. It is an interpretation of a film.
A papyrus describes forty-eight surgical cases with examinations, diagnoses and treatments, including the brain.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The legend of a city of gold began as a ritual: a Muisca chief covered in gold dust, offering at a lake. Expeditions killed thousands looking for a place that was never there.

Children's videos on YouTube were infiltrated by content with inappropriate themes, surfaced by recommendation. The scandal was real, the platform response was documented, and the underlying problem has not gone away.
The claim that thinking is shaped by having a body — that concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. It is well supported in some domains and over-claimed in others.
The proposal that gravity is not fundamental but arises from deeper physics, as temperature arises from atoms.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: California's electricity market was deregulated, and traders found ways to make money by creating scarcity. The state had rolling blackouts, and Enron collapsed.
First the platform is good to you, then it is good to its business customers, then it is good to nobody but its shareholders. The pattern is real; the law is not.
The proposal that gravity is not a fundamental force but an emergent consequence of entropy. It is elegant, it made a testable prediction, and the test disagreed.
The claim that trauma leaves chemical marks on DNA that pass to children and grandchildren. The human studies are small and confounded; the mechanism is real in animals and unproven in people.
The proposal that wormholes and quantum entanglement are the same phenomenon, described by two different theories. It is elegant, influential and unproved.
A librarian in Alexandria calculated the circumference of the Earth from a shadow and a distance, and got within a few per cent. The method is documented.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A set of videos with hidden codes that pointed, apparently, at a fast-food chain. The codes are real; the meaning is not settled.
The claim that Inuit languages have hundreds of words for snow. The number was invented by a populariser and has been repeated ever since.
Beneath fifteen kilometres of ice, Europa has more liquid water than all of Earth's oceans. Whether anything lives in it is unknown, and a spacecraft is on its way to look.
A theory that the series repeats, with the same events happening again and again. The show's ending is strange enough to support several readings.
The theory that the show's plot is driven by a statistical curve of Mortys. It is a joke about narrative and it is treated as one.
The claim that the mind is a collection of specialised modules shaped by Pleistocene selection. It is productive and contested, and the evidence for specific modules is thinner than the framework.
The claim that the Earth has grown over time, with the continents fitting together on a smaller globe. Plate tectonics explains the same fit without the growth.
A vision of wheels within wheels, read by some as a description of a spacecraft. The text is a prophetic vision.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Internal studies found harms to teenage users, and the company's own researchers said so. The documents were disclosed by a whistleblower.
Holding a pen in your teeth makes cartoons funnier, according to a 1988 study. A 17-lab replication failed to find it, and the argument since has been about what that means.
A joke that the series' characters have become superheroes, and that the films record a mutation. It is a description of escalation, not a plot.

Millisecond flashes of radio energy from other galaxies, first dismissed as a microwave oven and now observed in their thousands. The phenomenon is documented; the source of most of them is still open.
Senior football officials were indicted in the United States for racketeering and bribery over media and marketing rights. The president resigned.
A disc with the North Pole at the centre, a wall of ice at the rim, and a dome overhead. The model is simple. What is interesting is how it survives.
The story of a glass that could be bent, and an inventor executed to protect the gold trade. It is a legend with no evidence.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A city switched its water source to save money, and the water corroded the pipes. The lead poisoning is documented.
The claim that water fluoridation calcifies the pineal gland and dulls the mind. The studies cited are high-dose animal work, and the doses are orders of magnitude above drinking water.

A delusion shared by two people in a close relationship, usually one dominant and one suggestible. It is rare, it is real, and the modern diagnostic manuals have quietly stopped calling it a separate illness.
Fast radio bursts are real and unexplained. The proposal that they are alien light sails is the weakest of the options.
The theory that Tarzan is Anna and Elsa's brother, shipwrecked as a baby. It rests on a ship, a timeline and a set of parents who look similar.
Billions in customer deposits were lent to a trading firm run by the founder's girlfriend, moved through code exemptions, and spent on venture bets and real estate.
An exchange took customer deposits and lent them to a related trading firm, using a hidden exemption in its accounting. It collapsed in days.
In December 2022 the National Ignition Facility got more energy out of a fusion target than the laser delivered. Headlines said fusion had arrived. The grid is still waiting.
The theory that Inspector Gadget is a decoy while his niece does the work. It is a joke about the show's structure, and the show's structure supports it.

d.l: A metaphor that became a science
d.s: The Earth regulates its own temperature, chemistry and atmosphere as if it were alive. The strong version is wrong, the weak version is now mainstream, and the argument between them created Earth system science.
The proposal that life regulates the planet's conditions. The weak version is mainstream; the strong version is not.
A character in Undertale who exists only in fragments of the game's code and lore. The fragments are real; the character is a designed mystery.
A creepypasta about a sensory deprivation experiment that goes wrong. It is written as a case report, and the report is the fiction.
An analog horror series presented as a catalogue of home videos about nature, which turns out to be about something else.
Genes that move between species, not just from parent to child. Horizontal transfer is documented; its importance is argued.
The khan asked to be buried without a mark, and the location has been secret for eight centuries. Searches have been conducted, and the Mongolian government has stopped them.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Eurasia has more domesticable plants, more large animals and a long east–west axis. That is true and important. Whether it explains which countries are rich today is another question.

A French chemist proposed that the pyramid's blocks were cast from a limestone geopolymer rather than quarried. The idea explains some odd features and is contradicted by others, and the argument has been running for forty years.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Did language begin in the hands or the mouth? The evidence is indirect, and the debate has moved with discoveries about mirror systems, sign languages and ape gestures.
There is a race of giants in the oldest stories we have. There is also a ten-foot gypsum corpse in a New York field, sold for $23,000, and a mastodon thigh-bone that looked like a man.
A claim that the tomb of Gilgamesh was found under the Euphrates. The structure is real; the identification is a reading.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The law is a one-line summary of a century of institutional failure, and it is demonstrated every year.
A great ape described by Western science in 1847, and known to the peoples who lived beside it for far longer.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A model in which civilisations expand at a fixed speed and announce themselves, and the fact that we see none constrains when they appear. It explains the Fermi paradox by predicting we are early.
Experiments small enough for a laboratory bench now probe gravity itself. The measurements are real and the anomalies are not.
A Byzantine incendiary that burned on water and was projected from ships. The recipe was a state secret, and it was kept: nobody knows exactly what it was.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Self-replicating nanobots that consume the biosphere. It comes from a 1986 book about molecular manufacturing, and the physics of building it has never been demonstrated.
Why do animals help each other? Hamilton's rule explains a lot, and the argument about group selection has never quite ended.
Believing that ability can grow is a defensible idea with a small, real effect. Believing it is a lever that raises attainment for everyone is a claim that failed its largest test.
The Grand Theft Auto games are split into a 3D universe and an HD universe, with separate continuities. Rockstar confirmed it, and it explains why the same city looks different.
A terraced hill in Indonesia was claimed in 2023 to be a 25,000-year-old pyramid. Geologists and archaeologists have challenged the dating and the interpretation.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Carved pillars, sixteen tonnes each, built by people without pottery or farming. The date is settled. What the enclosures were for is not.

A research facility in Alaska heats a patch of the upper atmosphere with radio waves. It has been blamed for earthquakes, hurricanes and mind control, and its power output is smaller than a large city's.
Hair and nails do not grow after death. The skin recedes and creates the illusion.

Encrypted traffic is being recorded today so it can be read when quantum computers are able to break the encryption. It is not a theory about the future; it is guidance from the agencies, and a migration that is already under way.
Diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and cognitive problems, and some heard a sound. Eight years of investigation have produced two rival explanations and no confirmed cause.
Twin and adoption studies put the heritability of adult IQ high. What that number means, and what it does not, is where the argument lives.
A sphere turned by steam, described by Hero of Alexandria. It is a real device and it was not used for work.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that Nefertiti's tomb lies behind the walls of Tutankhamun's burial chamber, based on radar scans. The scans were repeated, and the chambers were not there.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The shell has an 800-mile wall. The polar openings are 1,400 miles wide. There is a small sun in the middle, and someone has always just come back from there.
If space is a hologram, it should jitter at the Planck scale. A purpose-built interferometer looked for the jitter and found nothing, which ruled out some versions of the idea.
A metre-tall hominin found on Flores, dated to as recently as 50,000 years ago. The discovery was disputed for a decade and is now accepted.
Birds, turtles and bacteria navigate by the Earth's field. The mechanism is still argued.
Out of Africa, with interbreeding and multiple dispersals. The broad picture is settled and the details are not.
Pterosaurs were the size of giraffes and flew. The leading explanation is a quadrupedal launch, using the wings as front legs to vault into the air.
A Mars-sized body hit the young Earth and the debris became the Moon. The broad picture is accepted; the isotope evidence has been making it complicated for twenty years.

Allergies and autoimmune disease rose through the twentieth century in rich countries. The explanation is not dirt, and the leading version — that we have lost contact with old microbial companions — has good evidence and no complete mechanism.

The white paper was 57 pages of enthusiasm. The hard parts were not the magnets; they were the tube, the thermal expansion, the safety case and the fact that a train needs to carry enough people to pay for itself.
Adam Curtis's argument that politics has become a managed spectacle. It is a documentary essay, and it is argued as one.
A diagnosis applied to women for two thousand years, and removed from the manuals in 1980.
One theory says consciousness is integrated information, wherever it occurs. The other says it is information broadcast widely in the brain. Both made predictions, and both were tested.
The claim that consciousness as people describe it — the felt quality of experience — is an illusion produced by the brain. It is a serious position and it is hard to state without sounding absurd.
Private browsing does not stop websites, employers or networks from seeing what you do. A lawsuit forced the clarification.
Inflation is the standard answer to 'why is the universe so uniform?' — and it is also the theory its critics say can explain almost anything, which is the problem.
A city in the Qur'an destroyed for its arrogance, and a byword for a lost city in the desert. A site in Oman has been excavated, and the identification is argued.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The US sold arms to Iran and used the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan rebels, in defiance of an embargo and a congressional ban. It was exposed, investigated and pardoned.
Wheeler's proposal that physical reality derives from information. It is a slogan with a programme behind it.
The theory that Jack Sparrow is a time traveller, based on his modern mannerisms. It is a reading of a performance, not a plot.
The claim that Jesus survived the crucifixion and travelled to Kashmir. It rests on a nineteenth-century book and no evidence.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A forum poster in 2000 claimed to be a time traveller from 2036. His predictions failed, his physics did not work, and the posts have been traced to a group of people.

A meaningful coincidence with no causal connection, offered as an acausal principle of nature. The concept names something people experience; as a claim about the world it cannot be tested, which is the problem.
A temple cut from the top of a hill downward, removing everything that is not the building. The method is documented by the marks left behind.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A YouTube series that turned an imageboard joke into a film. It is fiction, made by a named creator, and it has a studio deal.
A fan-made role-playing game with a hidden room that led players to a real website and a recruitment pitch for a 'clone' cult.
If growth continues at any plausible rate, the Milky Way is a few tens of millions of years of work. The galaxy is 13 billion years old. The silence is a statement about bottlenecks.
The scale of civilisations by energy use, extended far past anything observable.
A Wikipedia editor whose article about an invented painter became a real artwork, and a real exhibition.
The joke that Keanu Reeves has not aged because he is immortal, supported by portraits that look like him. The portraits are a selection, and the joke is the point.
Enough collisions in low orbit could produce a cascade that makes the region unusable for centuries. The mechanism is real; whether the cascade has started is argued.
The theory that the boy in Home Alone grew up to be the killer in Saw. It is a joke that got elaborate, and it is not in either film.
The theory that the pink character's games are secretly about an eldritch being. The lore is real; the horror framing is a reading.

d.t: Kitty Genovese and the Bystander Effect
d.s: A murder said to have been witnessed by 38 people who did nothing. The number was wrong; the effect is real but smaller.
The Minoan palace excavated by Arthur Evans, reconstructed in concrete, and argued about ever since.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: Kubrick Confessed to the Moon Hoax
d.s: A video appears to show Stanley Kubrick confessing to faking the Moon landings. The video is a hoax, the interview is real and unrelated, and the claim has been circulating since 2015.
A lost Tamil landmass said to have sunk south of India, sometimes linked to Lemuria. The ocean floor has been mapped, and there is no continent there.
A website and a Reddit thread that appeared to be a front for something. The documents are real; the interpretation is not settled.
A crater lake in Cameroon released a cloud of carbon dioxide that killed about 1,700 people overnight. It is the clearest documented case of a limnic eruption.
The universe was created last Thursday, complete with your memories, the fossils, and this website. It is not a claim anyone believes. It is a machine for showing what evidence cannot do.
A man who said he worked on alien craft at Area 51 claimed their fuel was element 115, unknown at the time. Element 115 was synthesised in 2003, and it decays in milliseconds.
Violent crime fell through the 1990s in every rich country at once, and nobody predicted it. One explanation is that a generation stopped breathing leaded petrol as children.
The claim that increased intestinal permeability allows bacterial products into the blood and drives systemic disease. The permeability is measurable; the disease claims are much larger.
A subgroup on low-carbohydrate diets shows large rises in LDL cholesterol while remaining lean and metabolically healthy. Whether that is harmless is the question.

The idea that children learn better when taught in their preferred mode — visual, auditory, kinaesthetic — is one of the most widely held beliefs in education and one of the most thoroughly tested negatives in psychology.
The idea that people are logical or creative by hemisphere. The hemispheres do differ, and not like that.
There is always a prime between n² and (n+1)². It has been checked far out and proved nowhere.
Straight lines drawn between ancient sites, said to be channels of earth energy. They are drawn after the fact.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Traders manipulated the interest rate that underpinned trillions in loans and derivatives, by submitting figures that suited their books.

The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead. Fifty kilometres up, the pressure and temperature are almost Earth-like — which is why the cloud layer keeps being proposed as a habitat, and why the phosphine claim of 2020 mattered.
The claim that life appeared on Mars before Earth, and came here on a rock. The mechanism is possible; the evidence is not there.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Lakes beneath Antarctica's ice sheet have been sealed for millions of years. Drilling them is a test of whether life persists in isolation.

d.t: Light Speed as a Clock Limit
d.s: The claim that the speed of light is not a physical constant but the processing limit of a simulation. The constant is measured; the simulation is an interpretation.
Does a photon's momentum in a medium follow Minkowski's or Abraham's formula? The argument ran for a century.
An aesthetic of empty corridors, read by some as a glimpse of what comes after. The images are real; the reading is fiction.
The script of Minoan Crete, used for accounting and ritual, and never deciphered. Linear B was cracked because a scholar guessed the language; Linear A has no such handle.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Does the language you speak shape what you can think? The strong version is dead; the weak version has small, replicated effects that are easy to overstate.
The choice at the end of a game about cycles. It is a reading of a fiction, and the fiction is about reading.
A baby conditioned to fear a white rat. The study is famous, the child was never identified, and the ethics were appalling.
A series of fictional emergency broadcasts, made as analog horror. The format borrows the authority of public information films.
A theory in which space itself is quantised into a network of finite loops. It is mathematically developed, predicts almost nothing measurable, and is one of the two main attempts at quantum gravity.

Lemuria was invented to explain where lemurs came from. Within twenty years it was a civilisation of telepathic giants who kept dinosaurs as pets. The real drowned continents are stranger in a quieter way.
The claim that the Soviet Union lost cosmonauts in orbit and covered it up, based on amateur radio recordings. The archives opened, and the crews are accounted for.
People can know they are dreaming while asleep, and say so from inside the dream. That was verified with eye movements in 1980, which makes it one of the few dream claims with a laboratory receipt.
A theory that the mysterious Board in Severance is the company's founder, still directing the firm. It is a reading of the show's theology.
A sunken kingdom off Cornwall, drowned in a single night, from which Tristan came. It is literature, and the sea floor has been surveyed.
Mutual assured destruction is the most consequential theory ever adopted without a controlled test. It has one data point in its favour and dozens of near-failures against.
Cut a magnet in half and you get two magnets. Nobody has ever found an isolated north pole. That absence is one of the most informative null results in physics.

Animals navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. That much is settled by decades of behavioural experiments. How a biological cell measures a field a hundred thousand times weaker than a fridge magnet is not.
A set of documents supposedly signed by Truman, establishing a secret committee on recovered alien craft. The FBI examined them and called them fake, and the forgery is not subtle.
Surveys find that a substantial share of men report no close friends and rely on a partner for emotional support. The pattern is documented; the explanations are contested.
Hot rock rising from deep in the mantle is the standard explanation for Hawaii and Iceland. The seismic evidence for the plumes is weaker than the theory requires.

This is the one entry in the archive that is not a fringe claim at all. It is a serious, taught, published interpretation of quantum mechanics — and it still does not mean what the internet says it means.
A YouTube series presented as found footage, made by three people, and one of the founding works of the Slender Man mythos.
The claim that tall ice cliffs at the edge of Antarctica could collapse rapidly, raising sea level faster than models allow. Later work suggests the cliffs are stronger than the hypothesis assumed.
A fan theory holds that Super Mario Bros. 3 is staged as a theatre performance — the curtain, the blocks on stands, the card at the end. It is a reading, and the developers have answered it.
If prices already contain all available information, nobody can beat the market except by luck. Half a century of tests has produced both support and a list of exceptions that refuse to go away.
Hundreds of Usenet posts in 1996 containing strings of words with no meaning. The posts are archived; their purpose is not known.
Marvel cast Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom after playing Iron Man. The decision is documented; the reasoning is the studio's.

Four hundred people danced until they collapsed in Strasbourg in 1518. The municipal records survive. This is the best-documented case in history of a symptom spreading through a crowd faster than any pathogen.
A proposed condition in which mast cells release mediators inappropriately, producing flushing, pain and allergic-type symptoms. The cells are real; the syndrome's criteria are contested.
A dating service that sent messages from fake accounts to lure users back. The regulator documented it.
A computer the size of a solar system, built in nested shells that each use the waste heat of the one inside. It is a thought experiment about thermodynamics, and nothing in the sky looks like one.
A pigment that survived a thousand years of tropical rain, and whose chemistry was only explained in the twentieth century.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The promotional game was rigged for years by the man who ran its security, who sold the winning pieces. The FBI investigation is documented.
A creepypasta told through a series of unsettling videos and posts. It is fiction, and the format is the work.
The gorgon's head turns viewers to stone. Explanations have included fossils, masks and ritual, and none is established.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A giant shark known from teeth, extinct for millions of years, said to survive in the deep ocean. The size of the animal is the argument against it.
Liquid mercury was found in a tunnel under the Feathered Serpent pyramid. It is documented, and it is not evidence of anything exotic.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that mica sheets in Egyptian monuments served an electrical purpose. Mica is present; the electrical use is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Microplastics are everywhere, including in blood and placentas. Whether they act as endocrine disruptors in people is a question the exposure data cannot yet answer.
A theory that a character's journey ends in death rather than return. It is an interpretation of a film.
The experiments that seemed to show ordinary people would follow orders to hurt strangers. The archives complicate the result.

Scan a brain at sufficient resolution, run the simulation, and the person continues in software. The proposal has a serious engineering roadmap and no working example, and the philosophical problem is not the engineering.
New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992 and Pennsylvania did not. The study that compared them overturned a textbook, and every study since has been arguing with it.
Every particle could have a mirror twin in a hidden sector that interacts only gravitationally. It would be dark matter, and it would be invisible. It is an elegant idea with no detection.

Neurons that fire both when a monkey acts and when it watches the same action. They were found in macaques, and the human claims built on them — empathy, language, autism — are much larger than the evidence.
A claim that Mithraic iconography encodes the precession of the equinoxes. The imagery is real; the astronomy is a reading.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A government that borrows in a currency it prints can always pay. That is arithmetic, not ideology. What follows from it — and what does not — is where the fight is.
A large animal said to live in the Congo basin, often described as a sauropod dinosaur. Expeditions have been going for a century and have produced stories, not specimens.
One constant, 10⁻¹⁰ metres per second squared, and a rule: below that acceleration, gravity pulls harder than Newton says. It fits galaxies beautifully and clusters badly.
The world's most famous property game was invented to teach that land monopolies are unjust. The irony is documented in patents and in the inventor's own words.
Internal documents showed the company drafting research on its own products and arranging for academics to publish it.
A minor character read as the series' hidden controller. It is an interpretation of a game.
A letter to a medical journal created a condition. Blinded trials did not find it.

The claim that intelligence comes in eight or nine independent kinds reshaped classrooms worldwide. As a description of how abilities are organised it does not survive the data, and the theory was never built to be tested.
A joke that the Muppets are legally citizens with rights. It is a joke about puppets, and it is filed as one.
There are people whose bones will not break, people who can see a colour you cannot, and populations that function where visitors vomit and lose consciousness. None of them glow.
A Doom level released with a story about a friend who died. It is a work of art in a 1993 game engine, and it is fiction.
A French physicist discovered a new radiation that only he could detect. It did not exist.
A city built on artificial islets from stacked basalt columns, in a lagoon in Micronesia. It is real, and it took centuries.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The equations that describe fluid flow are used every day and have never been proved to have solutions that stay smooth. Turbulence is the reason it matters.
The lines and figures on the Nazca desert were said to be landing strips for aircraft. They are shallow scrapes in the surface, and the ground beneath them would not support a wheel.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Bones from several Neanderthal sites carry cut marks and fractures consistent with butchery. The evidence is direct, and the interpretation is not.
People brought back from cardiac arrest report tunnels, light, life review and calm. The reports are real and consistent enough to study. What they mean about death is the part that is not.
The claim that the brain releases DMT at death, producing the tunnel, the light and the life review. The resemblance is real; the release has never been measured.
The name in Finding Nemo means 'nobody' in Latin, which is either a coincidence or the film's central joke. The etymology is documented; the intent is not.
Skulls with holes cut into them, and bone regrowth showing that some people survived. The surgery is documented; the motive is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Nero was said to have fiddled while Rome burned, and to have started the fire to clear space for his palace. The first is impossible and the second is unlikely.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claimed law that would cancel all debt, abolish income tax and deliver prosperity packages. It has been 'about to be announced' for thirty years.

Environmental DNA sampling of Loch Ness found eel DNA in most samples and no reptilian DNA at all. The eel hypothesis is the most parsimonious one on offer, which is not the same as evidence for a giant eel.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: The Loch Ness Monster is usually drawn as a plesiosaur. That identification has a specific problem: a breeding population of large air-breathing reptiles in a cold lake would leave traces, and none has been found.

d.t: New Coke as a Trojan Horse
d.s: Coca-Cola replaced its recipe in 1985, the public revolted, and the original returned in 79 days. The claim is that the whole thing was a planned manoeuvre.
A passage tomb in Ireland aligned so that the rising sun at midwinter reaches the chamber floor. The alignment is measured every year.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claimed planet on a long orbit that would pass Earth. It has been predicted repeatedly and has never appeared.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A man builds a boat, loads the animals, and the world is drowned. The story is older than the Bible, and the geology is younger than the story.
A creepypasta about a haunted house with a series of rooms and no exit. It is fiction, and its structure has been widely copied.

A 2023 congressional hearing was told the United States holds craft and biological material of non-human origin. The claim is consequential, the evidence has not been produced, and the official investigations have found nothing to support it.
Novels were said to corrupt young women and drive them mad. The claim is documented; the evidence never existed.
A depression in the ground, a story about pirate gold, and 230 years of men bankrupting themselves to find it. The pit is real. The treasure is the part nobody has produced.

A Babylonian priest described a fish-man who came out of the sea and taught civilisation. It is a myth recorded centuries after the fact, and it has become a fixture of the ancient-astronaut literature.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Standard quantum theory says the wavefunction collapses when measured, and never says what a measurement is. Objective-collapse models replace that with real physics: the collapse happens on its own.
Europa, Enceladus, Titan, Ganymede, Ceres: subsurface oceans may be common. Whether they are habitable is another question.
A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors. Every one known is even, and nobody knows whether an odd one exists.
A claim that Inca stonework at Ollantaytambo shows machine cutting. The precision is real; the machines are not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: One Piece and the All Blue
d.s: A theory about where a legendary sea is. It is an interpretation of a long-running manga.
A closed model can be withdrawn. An open one cannot. That single asymmetry drives most of the argument, and neither side disputes it.
US agents allowed firearms to be trafficked into Mexico in order to trace them, and lost track of most of them. Two were found at the scene of a Border Patrol agent's killing.
A US naval expedition to Antarctica in 1946–47, with 4,700 men and a carrier. It has been read as a military operation against a hidden Nazi or alien base.
The Church of Scientology ran a systematic infiltration of US government offices to remove documents about itself. Eleven senior officials were convicted.
The film dramatises a fear that the first test might ignite the atmosphere. The fear was real, the calculation was done, and the answer was no.
The claim that consciousness arises from quantum computation in microtubules inside neurons. It has a testable prediction, one experiment that claimed to support it, and no replication.
Is every problem whose answer can be checked quickly also solvable quickly? Almost everyone believes not, and nobody can prove it.
Analysing data in many ways until a result appears, and reporting only that. The practice is documented and measurable.
A lost Inca city said to lie east of the Andes. Expeditions have searched; nothing has been found.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The carved lid of Pakal's sarcophagus at Palenque shows a figure in a complex posture. In 1968 it was read as an astronaut in a spaceship, which requires ignoring the Maya iconography around it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that a streptococcal infection can trigger sudden obsessive-compulsive symptoms in children. The clinical phenomenon is described; the autoimmune mechanism is not established.

The view that experience is a basic feature of matter, not something that emerges from complexity. It is taken seriously by a minority of philosophers, has no test, and is not the same as saying rocks are conscious.
Organisations that sell authorship on fabricated papers. Their output is documented in the published record.
Millions of people talk to chatbots as companions. The attachment is real and measurable; whether it is good for them is genuinely unsettled, and the companies selling it are not running the trials.
In 1966 Paul McCartney died in a car crash and the Beatles replaced him with a lookalike, hiding clues in their album covers. The man himself has been asked about it for fifty years.
Peer review is the gatekeeping ritual of science, and the evidence that it works is thinner than most people assume.
No link to tap, no app to install. A crafted message arrives and the phone is compromised — journalists, lawyers, activists and heads of state on the list.
Spyware that infects a phone without any interaction, sold to governments. The 2021 Pegasus Project documented its use against journalists, lawyers and activists.
The proposal that the universe repeats in aeons, with evidence claimed in the cosmic microwave background. The claims have not held.
People reached the Americas before the last glacial maximum or after it, by land or by coast. The dates have been moving earlier for thirty years.
A blue whale has a thousand times more cells than you. By the arithmetic of random mutation, it should die of cancer almost immediately. It lives a century.
A YouTube series presenting footage of a nonexistent 1990s PlayStation game. The game was never made, and the story is in the editing.
Charlemagne never existed, and 297 years of the early Middle Ages were invented by two men who wanted to live in the year 1000. It is a seductive story, and dendrochronology alone ends it.
The phone buzzes in a pocket that has no phone in it. Most people who carry one have felt it, and it is a textbook case of a learned association misfiring.
The joke theory that Phoebe in Friends is homeless and sleeps in the coffee shop. It is contradicted by the show, and it is funny.
One absorption line, 20 parts per billion, and a gas that on Earth is made by life. The follow-up work has been brutal — and the story is not quite over.
The claim that personality could be read from the shape of the skull. It was wrong, and it seeded real neuroscience.
A generation remembers Pikachu with a black tip on its tail. It has never had one, and the false memory is a textbook case.
Bohmian mechanics says the electron really is somewhere, and the wavefunction really does push it. Every experimental prediction matches ordinary quantum theory, because the maths is the same.
The placebo effect is real, and it is not one thing: expectation, conditioning, regression and reporting bias all contribute, and the size depends on the outcome.
A handful of icy bodies beyond Neptune share an odd alignment. Either a planet five to ten times Earth's mass shepherds them, or the solar system is playing a statistical trick.

d.t: Planet Nine as a Black Hole
d.s: Something is perturbing distant solar system objects. One proposal is a planet; another is a primordial black hole of a few Earth masses. Both are inference from orbits, and neither has been seen.
Plants signal, remember in a loose sense, and respond to damage. The claim that they have nervous systems, or brains, is where the metaphor stops being useful.
Without a clear marker of intent, a parody of extremism is indistinguishable from the real thing. It was formulated on a forum and has been demonstrated repeatedly since.
Polynesians settled the Pacific without instruments, using stars, swells, birds and clouds. The claim that they did it deliberately was dismissed for centuries and then demonstrated.

A theory that the vagus nerve supports three hierarchical states — social engagement, fight-or-flight, shutdown — and that trauma traps people in the lower ones. It is enormously popular in therapy and weakly supported in physiology.
A form of water said to be denser and more viscous, with extraordinary properties. It was contaminated ordinary water.
Two towns buried by Vesuvius, preserving streets, food, graffiti and a library of carbonised scrolls.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: Portal and Half-Life Share a Universe
d.s: Two Valve games set in the same world, with a research ship, a shadowy corporation and a shared apocalypse. The connection is documented in the games and confirmed by the studio.
Standing confidently was said to change your hormones and your risk appetite. The hormonal claim did not replicate.
Journals that charge authors and publish without real review. The category is documented and its boundaries are argued.
The claim that the brain is a prediction machine, constantly modelling the world and correcting the errors. It explains a lot and has been hard to prove.
Systems that send police where crime data says crime happens, which is where police have been sent before.
If the early universe was dense enough, it could have collapsed into black holes smaller than atoms. Some of them might still be here — and might be the missing mass.
Misfolded proteins that propagate through the brain, implicated in several neurodegenerative diseases. The mechanism is documented for prions; its reach is argued.
The US military tested biological and chemical agents on ships and in the open, sometimes without informing the personnel involved. The programme was disclosed decades later.
The CIA built a ship to lift a sunken Soviet submarine from the Pacific floor, and told the world it was mining manganese. It is the most expensive covert engineering project of the Cold War.
A Titan stole fire for humanity and was punished. The story has been read as an account of a visitor who gave technology to humans. It is a myth about knowledge and its cost.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The world has ended, on schedule, hundreds of times. The interesting question is not why the predictions fail — it is what the believers do on the Monday afterwards.
Real conspiracies exist, and they are on the record. That is precisely why the unfalsifiable ones are recognisable: they look nothing like this.
Studies that find nothing are less likely to be published, so the literature overstates effects. The bias is measured, not suspected.
Stone blocks at Tiwanaku have precise right angles and interlocking shapes, said to require lasers. They were cut with stone tools, and the site has been heavily disturbed.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The fossil record shows long stretches of nothing followed by sudden change. Whether that is how evolution works, or how rocks record it, is still argued.
A company marketed an addictive opioid as low-risk, using a claim about its formulation that was not supported. The consequences are measured in deaths.
A Greek navigator sailed to Britain, described sea ice and a frozen sea, and was disbelieved for centuries.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: An interpretation in which the quantum state is a person's expectation, not a fact about the world.
The First Emperor's tomb is said to contain rivers of mercury under a ceiling of pearls. The soil around the mound shows elevated mercury, and the tomb has never been opened.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: In 2019 a quantum processor finished a sampling task in minutes that would take a classical supercomputer millennia. Within five years, classical methods had closed much of the gap.
Light-harvesting complexes were reported to sustain quantum coherence for hundreds of femtoseconds. Whether that coherence helps, or is a by-product, is the argument.
Why do we and the environment agree about what a measurement found? Quantum Darwinism answers: because the environment keeps many copies, and only some states get copied.

The claim that consciousness can direct quantum processes to heal the body. It uses the vocabulary of quantum mechanics, and every one of its central assertions contradicts what quantum mechanics says about warm, wet tissue.
Two of the strangest things physicists have said about electrons and death: you can never experience your own, and there may only be one electron in the universe.
The claim that we smell by detecting molecular vibrations through quantum tunnelling, rather than by shape. The evidence is mixed and the debate is live.
A feathered serpent god was recast in the twentieth century as a pale-skinned teacher from overseas. The evidence for the visitor is a sixteenth-century text read backwards.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A volcanic winter darkened the sun for eighteen months, and Norse legend describes a winter with no summer. The parallel is suggestive.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Reports of fish, frogs and other animals falling from the sky are documented across centuries. The mechanism is meteorological, and it is well understood.

An app that generates a random coordinate and sends you there, promising 'anomalies'. In 2020 two teenagers following one found a suitcase containing human remains, and the app became famous for the wrong reason.
Is complex life rare because Earth is unusual, or ordinary because the galaxy is vast? Both arguments are principled and neither is settled.
Downs noticed in 1957 that a self-interested voter should stay home. Sixty years of research has produced four kinds of answer, and no consensus on which one describes actual voters.

In 1983 Benjamin Libet measured a slow build-up of brain activity starting a few hundred milliseconds before subjects reported deciding to move. It has been cited as proof that free will is an illusion ever since.
A practice, spread on TikTok, of moving consciousness to another reality by relaxing into sleep. It is a description of dreaming with a different vocabulary and a stronger claim.
The proposal that quantum states are always relative to an observer, and that there is no observer-independent description.
The claim that reality only renders what is observed, as a game engine does. The observation is real; the engine is a metaphor.

The claim that traumatic memories can be pushed out of awareness and recovered later, often in therapy. The evidence for the mechanism is weak, and the recovered memories have produced both convictions and miscarriages of justice.
The proposal that later events can influence earlier ones. Some interpretations use it; no experiment has shown it.

d.t: Richard III Under a Car Park
d.s: The last Plantagenet king was buried in a friary that became a car park. His skeleton was found in 2012, under a marked parking bay.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Two answers to how life began: a self-replicating molecule, or a self-sustaining chemical network. Both have support and neither is demonstrated.
A future AI will torture anyone who knew it was coming and did nothing to help. You have now read about it. That last sentence is the entire mechanism.
Roman marine concrete has survived two thousand years of seawater. The explanation is lime clasts that crack, dissolve and recrystallise — and a 2023 study found a way to make it deliberately.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Hollow bronze objects with twelve pentagonal faces and knobs at the corners, found across the northern provinces. Nobody knows what they were for.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Roman coins are found in India, and a Roman-era text describes the monsoon route. The trade was large enough to worry Roman writers.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A script from Easter Island, carved on wooden tablets, and undeciphered. Only about two dozen objects survive.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A room in an AT&T switching centre in San Francisco, built for the NSA, where internet traffic was copied. A technician's evidence exposed it in 2006.
A material that carries current with no resistance would rebuild the electrical grid. The physics is real; the room-temperature claims have not survived.
The 1947 Roswell debris was a secret balloon array built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The US Air Force said so in 1994, and the alien story arrived decades later.

A family of bankers has been at the centre of conspiracy theories for two centuries. The theories are documented as theories, and they are false — and they repeat a familiar pattern of antisemitic tropes.
A 2015 horror game distributed through the deep web, said to contain illegal material. The claims are unverified, the game has been examined, and its authorship is unknown.
A lost anime said to show children trapped in a bathroom. It has never been found, and the search suggests it never existed.
Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, and the story says the ground was sown with salt so nothing would grow. The salt is a modern invention.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator was a state intelligence operation. The identity is unknown, and the claim is an inference from the design.
The central claim of modern dietary advice, and the subject of a long, documented argument.
Double the parameters and the loss drops by a predictable amount, across seven orders of magnitude. Then the awkward part: loss is not capability, and the smooth curves stop being smooth.
The bet was $1,000 on five metals over ten years. Simon won, Ehrlich paid, and the argument has continued as if the bet had not happened.
The SCP Foundation is a collaborative fiction wiki. The claim that it is a real agency with real containment procedures is a misunderstanding of a very consistent joke.

A fictional creature that becomes violently distressed when its face is seen. It is one entry in a collaborative writing project with thousands of them, and it is labelled fiction everywhere it appears.

d.t: Screen Time and Teen Mental Health
d.s: Two camps, one dataset, opposite headlines. The honest summary is that screen use correlates weakly with well-being, that the correlation is smaller than nearly everything else in the same data, and that causality is unresolved.
The Illuminati existed for about ten years, was banned, had its papers seized and published — and has been running the world ever since, according to people who have never read the papers.

A city sprayed with bacteria, dead infants measured for fallout, a cat with a transmitter in its skull, a gun that causes heart attacks, and a proposal to make soldiers attracted to each other. All real documents.

If the interest rate that balances saving and investment is below zero, the central bank cannot reach it. Demand then falls short year after year, and the economy runs cool not because of a shock but because of its structure.
The claim that industrial seed oils cause inflammation through omega-6 fatty acids. The biochemistry is real; the clinical evidence does not support the harm.

The story that depression is caused by low serotonin is the most repeated claim in mental health. A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, and the argument since has been about what that means for the drugs.

Two people report the same dream on the same night. It is one of the most compelling experiences a person can have and one of the hardest claims to test, because dreams are private and reports are not.
Shaving does not change hair growth. The stubble only feels coarser.
The claim that short-form video has shortened attention spans. The evidence is mixed, the definition of attention is contested, and the platforms measure engagement, not cognition.
Products get smaller or worse while the price stays the same. Both are documented by statistics agencies, and both are hard for a shopper to see.
Roman and later glass found along Asian trade routes, showing how far goods travelled and how technology spread.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A ranch in Utah with a reputation for cattle mutilation, strange lights and 'portals'. It was investigated by a defence contractor and by a television series, with no published findings.
Internet posts claim that whistling at night attracts a skinwalker. The taboo is real in some traditions; the internet version is not.
People have committed violence while asleep, and courts have had to decide what that means.
The claim that Slender Man became real because enough people thought about him. He was invented in a forum contest in 2009, and the tulpa claim is part of the fiction.
The claim that smart-city projects are a cover for total surveillance. The sensors are real; the total grid is not, and the projects have mostly been smaller and duller.
Televisions that recognise what is on screen and report it. The feature is documented in patents, settings and research.
A creepypasta about an image that drives people mad. The image is a story element, and the story is the work.
Twice in the Neoproterozoic, ice reached sea level in the tropics. The evidence is in the rocks and is not seriously disputed; how the planet got out again is still argued about.
A 2021 paper argued that a site in Jordan was destroyed by a Tunguska-like airburst around 1650 BC, and linked it to Sodom. The claim is contested on chronology, geology and identification.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
