d.s: Cooling the planet by reflecting sunlight — sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere, or brighter clouds. The physics is understood, the governance is not, and the termination problem is the argument against.
A ritual drink praised in the Rigveda, and a botanical identification that has never been settled.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Sound makes a bubble collapse; the collapse emits a flash of light lasting picoseconds. The inside may be hotter than the surface of the Sun, and nobody can measure it directly.
Music CDs installed hidden software that compromised the computers of the people who bought them.
A dinosaur with a sail, a crocodile snout and dense bones, proposed as a swimmer. The 2020 tail find supported it; later work questioned whether it could dive.
Severing the connection between the hemispheres produced patients whose two halves seemed to know different things. Whether that means two minds is still argued.
A fan theory holds that the red and blue cards in Squid Game encode the choice between the games and the outside world. The show's creator has described the cards more simply.
A creepypasta about flights of stairs found in forests, leading nowhere. It began as an imageboard thread and became a genre fixture.
A gelatinous substance found in fields, traditionally said to fall from the sky during meteor showers. The DNA work has found frog and toad, and the rest is slime mould and bacteria.
A train of bright lights crosses the sky, and a town reports a UFO. It is a line of satellites catching the sun, and the reports are now a routine part of astronomy outreach.
The claim that reminding people of a negative stereotype about their group impairs their performance. It replicated in small studies and largely failed in large pre-registered ones.
A hypothetical neutrino that interacts only through gravity. Several anomalies pointed to it; the experiments have not confirmed it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that a blind musician is not blind. It is a joke that has been repeated as fact.
One camp says a language model is a curve-fitting machine that parrots its training data. The other says that to predict text well enough, it has to build a model of the world that produced it.
A claim that Inca masons softened stone with plant acids to fit it perfectly. The fit is real; the method is not established.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A replica of Stonehenge has been built and measured. The stones do affect sound in ways that would matter for speech, music and drumming — and the site is a ruin, which is the problem with every claim about how it sounded.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: In 1963 an astronomer argued that Stonehenge was a machine for predicting eclipses. The alignments are real; the machine is the part that did not survive scrutiny.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Two research programmes, one target: a theory of gravity that works at the Planck scale. They disagree about almost everything else, and neither has been tested.
A computer worm that destroyed uranium centrifuges in Iran by making them spin at the wrong speed while reporting normal operation. It is the first known cyber weapon to cause physical damage.
The claim that simulations nest inside simulations, so that our world is many layers down. The argument is statistical, and it has no empirical content.

Functionalism says a mind is defined by what it does, not what it is made of — so the same program would be conscious wherever it ran. That is either obvious or a category error, and the disagreement is about which.
The comparison between the Roy family and Shakespeare's tragedy is made constantly. It is a useful reading and it is not a hidden source.
Sugar does not make children hyperactive. Parents and blinded observers disagree, and that is the finding.
A drowned subcontinent in Southeast Asia, exposed at low sea levels, with a coastline the size of Europe's. It is real; what happened on it is the debate.
The proposal that quantum experiments violate Bell's inequalities because the settings were fixed in advance. It saves locality and gives up free choice.
In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma with a stranger, defecting is dominant. Unless the stranger is your mirror — in which case the choice is not what to do, but what kind of reasoner to be.
A symmetry between matter and force particles would solve several problems at once. The LHC was built partly to find it, and has found nothing. That is not the same as ruling it out.
A South American crop was being grown in Polynesia before Europeans arrived. Someone crossed the ocean with it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The rule that you must wait an hour after eating before swimming. There is no evidence for it.
For some people, letters have colours and sounds have tastes, consistently, for a lifetime. It is one of the few claims in this archive that a laboratory can check in an afternoon.
The claim that Tyrannosaurus was too slow and too small-eyed to hunt, and lived as a scavenger. The evidence points to an animal that did both.
A star 1,470 light years away keeps dimming in strange, uneven ways. A comet swarm was the first guess, dust the current one — and a megastructure was never more than a headline.
Particles that always travel faster than light. They are mathematically possible and physically absent.

A millimetre-long animal that survives vacuum, radiation and decades without water is real. The claim built on top of it — that life travels between planets — is a different proposition, and the experiments that get quoted do not support it.
Every old city has basement windows cut in half by the pavement. The theory says a civilisation of giants built the buildings, then a wall of mud buried the ground floors and the history books.
“As far beneath the earth as heaven is above it.” The Greeks gave the underworld a floor plan, a wall, a gate and a prisoner list. Everything after that is reuse.
A wealthy kingdom in southern Spain, described by Greek writers, that traded with the Phoenicians and then vanished. Its capital has never been found.

The claim that cloud platforms have replaced markets with rents, and that capitalism has been succeeded by something older in structure. It is a thesis about political economy, argued from data that is contested.
Every generation has been told that machines will end work, and every generation has been mostly wrong. That history is an argument, not a guarantee.
The idea that a civilisation could be detected by its pollution — nitrogen dioxide, chlorofluorocarbons, industrial waste — rather than by its radio.
A caving diary posted online in 2001, in which a narrow passage leads to something. It is one of the oldest creepypastas, and it was written as fiction.
The claim that awareness of death drives people toward cultural worldviews and self-esteem. It has hundreds of studies behind it, a replication problem, and a large theoretical apparatus.
A joke that the Soviet Union built Tetris as a psychological weapon. It was written by a programmer in 1984, and it was not.
A claim that urban planning proposals are a scheme to confine people. The proposals are real; the confinement is not.
Billions taken from a Malaysian state fund, traced through banks, films and a yacht. The prosecutions are documented.
A subreddit that posted strings of encrypted or random data for three years, with no explanation. The mystery is documented; the explanation is mundane.
A conjecture about the prime factors of a+b=c that would settle a family of Diophantine problems. A claimed proof has been disputed since 2012.
Thousands of ceramic figures showing humans with dinosaurs, said to be ancient. The dating and the context failed.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Advanced civilisations may be asleep, waiting for the universe to cool so their computers run more efficiently. It explains the absence of aliens by predicting it, which is either elegant or unfalsifiable.

A person role-plays an AI locked in a text-only box and tries to persuade a gatekeeper to release it. Two claimed successes are cited as evidence that containment would fail. They are anecdotes, not experiments.

An aluminium wedge was found in Romania in 1973 alongside bones, and was said to be ancient. Aluminium of that kind was not made before the nineteenth century, and the object is probably wartime debris.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A compendium of everything that has ever happened, said to be readable by the trained. It is a claim with no evidence, no mechanism and no test — and it shaped a great deal of modern spiritual writing.
The claim that food changes blood pH and that acidity causes disease. The body regulates pH within a narrow range.
Greek writers described warrior women. Archaeology has found women buried with weapons on the steppe.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A room panelled in amber, looted by the Nazis in 1941, and lost in 1945. The reconstruction is finished; the original is still missing, and the search has produced a great deal of theory and no amber.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A geometric object whose volume encodes particle-scattering probabilities. It works, and it is not yet physics in the usual sense.
Humans have changed the rock record. Whether that deserves a place in the geological timescale was put to a vote in 2024 and lost — and the vote is more interesting than the answer.
A bronze gear mechanism from a Roman-era shipwreck, built to model the heavens. Nothing of comparable complexity appears for a thousand years afterwards.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Sitchin's claim that alien visitors created humanity, built on a mistranslation of Sumerian texts.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Assyrian reliefs show fish-cloaked and bird-headed sages who brought the arts to humanity. They are the Mesopotamian originals behind Oannes, and they are mythological advisers, not visitors.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A human ancestor that took to the water would explain hairlessness, upright posture and the diving reflex in one stroke. The fossil record, the comparative anatomy and the genetics each say otherwise, and the charitable version of the idea is a different claim.
The Ark of the Covenant was a gold-plated box that killed a man who touched it. The claim is that it was an electrical capacitor. The description fits a capacitor; the rest does not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A church in Aksum claims to hold the Ark of the Covenant. The claim is a matter of faith, and no examination has been permitted.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: The Ark in the King's Chamber
d.s: A claim that the Ark of the Covenant was housed in the Great Pyramid. The chamber is real; the Ark is not there.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Every fundamental law of physics works the same played backwards. Cups break and do not unbreak. The asymmetry is real, and it is not in the equations.
A baseball team used a camera and a monitor to relay the opposing catcher's signals. The scheme is documented in a league report.
A pattern in the cosmic microwave background that seems to align with the solar system. It is probably a statistical artefact.
Learn a new word and it appears everywhere for a week. Nothing has changed except your attention — which is why it is also called the frequency illusion.
Noclip out of reality in the wrong place and you fall into six hundred million square miles of damp carpet and buzzing lights. It began as one photograph and one paragraph.

An endless maze of yellow rooms, invented in a 2019 forum post, expanded by thousands of writers and filmmakers. It is fiction, it is labelled, and it has become one of the defining images of the internet's sense of place.

A clay jar with a copper cylinder and an iron rod will produce a voltage if you fill it with vinegar. Whether anyone in Parthian Iraq did that is a different question, and the answer is almost certainly no.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Caves cut into granite in Bihar with polished surfaces and an echo that lasts for seconds. They were made for an ascetic sect, and the finish is documented.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A people with a language unrelated to any other in Europe, and a genetic history that is distinctive without being separate.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A stone with an inscription said to be Hebrew, found in a Tennessee mound. It is a nineteenth-century inscription, and it is upside down.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A generation remembers the books as 'Berenstein'. They were always 'Berenstain'. The spelling is the archive's neatest case of a false memory shared by thousands of people.
Ships and aircraft have been lost in the western Atlantic, as they have been lost everywhere. The triangle was assembled from a handful of famous cases, a bestseller, and an absence of denominator.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: A steel sphere found after a forest fire was said to move on its own, hum, and resist investigation. It is a ball bearing from industrial machinery.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Three thousand years ago, humans had no inner life. Their own thoughts arrived as the voices of gods, and they obeyed them. It is one of the most audacious books of the century, and the neuroscience does not support it.

If the universe contracts before it expands, the Big Bang is not a beginning. The idea is mathematically developed and observationally untested, and the cosmic microwave background is where it would show.
Hawking radiation carries no information about what fell in. If that is true, quantum mechanics is wrong; if it is false, relativity is. Fifty years of work has produced progress and no experiment.
An alien satellite in polar orbit for 13,000 years, photographed by NASA in 1998. The photograph is real. The object is a piece of insulation that drifted out of the shuttle's cargo bay.
A hypothesis that the Black Sea flooded catastrophically when the Mediterranean broke through. The flood is argued; its scale and date are not settled.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A supposed game that assigned self-harm tasks. No evidence of the game has been found; the panic caused real harm.
Hundreds of bodies have been recovered from northern European peat bogs, preserved by the chemistry of the peat. Many were killed deliberately.
Between about 1.8 and 0.8 billion years ago, the Earth's climate, oceans and evolution appear to have been unusually stable. Whether it was boring is now disputed.
Four hills near Visoko, said to be the largest human-made pyramids on Earth, older than Sumer. The shape is real. The construction is not.
A theory about a hidden faction in a game's city. It is an interpretation of a fiction.
A region of sky about 330 million light years across contains far fewer galaxies than it should. It is real, it is not empty, and it is not evidence of anything stranger than large-scale structure.
The Mahabharata describes celestial weapons of enormous destructive power. They have been read as nuclear bombs. They are literary devices in a poem about dharma.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Standing at a height, a small number of people feel a sudden urge to jump. It is not a death wish, it is common, and it has a name in French that predates the research.

Almost every major animal group appears in the fossil record within about twenty million years. Whether that is an explosion of life or an explosion of fossils is the argument, and it has been running since Darwin apologised for it.
The claim that obesity is driven by insulin, and that carbohydrate restriction is therefore uniquely effective. The trials find that, matched for protein and calories, the diets perform similarly.
Paid events where groups meditate to summon UFOs. Participants report lights in the sky; the lights are usually identifiable, and the protocol has never produced an object anyone could examine.
The claim that mental illness is caused by a chemical imbalance was told to patients for decades. It was a simplification, and the correction has been widely misread.
A lion with a goat's head and a serpent's tail, and a possible origin in volcanic landscape.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A person in a room follows rules for manipulating Chinese characters and produces perfect answers in Chinese. She understands nothing. Is the room a computer, or is this a story about what it feels like to be one?
The claim that 'crisis' in Chinese means danger plus opportunity. It does not.
A creature that drains livestock of blood, first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Every carcass that has been tested has turned out to be a coyote or dog with mange.
The CIA covertly funded abstract expressionist exhibitions and journals during the Cold War, as cultural diplomacy. The paintings were real; the funding was hidden.
The CIA recruited mafia figures to kill Fidel Castro, using poison pills, exploding cigars and a contaminated diving suit. The schemes failed, and the Church Committee published them.
A small Ohio town received anonymous letters accusing residents of affairs and worse. One man was convicted of a related crime; the letter-writer was never identified.
A fish known only from fossils, and thought extinct for 65 million years, was caught off South Africa in 1938. A second population was found in Indonesia in 1997.
Halve even numbers, triple-and-add-one odd ones, and you always reach 1. Nobody knows why, and Paul Erdős said mathematics is not ready for it.
Comic books were blamed for juvenile delinquency, and a Senate subcommittee and an industry code followed.

Intergroup contact reduces prejudice — one of the most replicated findings in social psychology. The dispute is about the conditions: equal status, shared goals, cooperation and institutional support, all of which are easy to state and hard to arrange.

One Dead Sea Scroll is not a text but a treasure map: sixty-four locations, quantities of gold and silver, and no treasure ever found. It is the only scroll in the collection that reads like an inventory.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: The Cosmic Web and the Brain
d.s: A 2020 paper compared the distribution of galaxies to the network of neurons in a brain, and found them quantitatively similar. The comparison is a real result about structure, not about consciousness.
A 'geode' from California was found to contain a spark plug. It was said to be half a million years old. It is a 1920s Champion spark plug in a concretion.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Two girls photographed fairies in a Yorkshire garden, and Sherlock Holmes's creator believed them. Sixty years later they admitted the fairies were paper cut-outs pinned to a bush.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: About four hundred pines near Gryfino in Poland bend sharply north at their base. They were planted in the 1930s, and nobody knows why they bend.

The Crystal Palace was a glass and iron building of unprecedented scale, and the idea of a 'crystal palace' became a utopian image. It has been read as evidence of lost technology rather than of Victorian engineering.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A dozen quartz skulls were said to be pre-Columbian, and one was said to be the work of aliens or Atlanteans. Microscopy found nineteenth-century lapidary tools on every one that has been examined.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A suggestion that the Cyclops story came from fossil elephant skulls, whose nasal opening looks like a single eye socket.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Washington's diagonal avenues are said to form a pentagram, a Masonic symbol and a satanic layout. They are baroque city planning, and the geometry does not work.
In Strasbourg, hundreds of people danced for days without stopping, and some died. The two leading explanations are ergot poisoning and mass psychogenic illness.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.l: A fiction premise, taken as a warning
d.s: The universe is a dark forest full of armed hunters. Make a sound, and something finds you. It is the most chilling answer to “where is everybody?” — and it was written as a novel.

d.l: Half-true, and the true half is worse
d.s: The claim: most of the internet is no longer people. The data does not support the total version — and the partial version is genuinely unsettling.
Manuscripts hidden in caves near Qumran, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical texts. They were found by Bedouin shepherds.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Microbes live in rock kilometres below the surface, and they may account for a large fraction of the planet's biomass. How much, and how active, is argued.

d.t: The Default Mode Network and Ego Death
d.s: Psychedelics reduce activity in the brain network associated with self-referential thought, and people report the dissolution of the self. The correlation is documented; the interpretation is not.
A theory that the oracle at Delphi was inspired by ethylene gas rising from a fault. The geology is real; the effect is argued.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A relief at Dendera shows a bulb-shaped object with a snake inside it. The claim that it depicts an electric lamp ignores the rest of the scene, which explains it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Hoof-like prints appeared across Devon overnight, in a line, over walls and roofs. The snow was real; the explanation is still argued.

An asteroid hit the Yucatán 66 million years ago and three quarters of species died. The argument about whether the impact or the Deccan volcanoes did it is now mostly an argument about timing, and the timing has been measured.
The Dogon of Mali are said to have known that Sirius has a tiny, dense companion with a fifty-year orbit, centuries before telescopes could see it. The fieldwork behind the claim is the problem.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: You were born somewhere in the human sequence, not at a special point in it. Apply that assumption and the numbers say the species probably ends within a few thousand years. The argument turns entirely on whether the assumption is legitimate.
A gas crater in Turkmenistan has been burning since 1971, and it looks like an entrance to the underworld. It is a collapsed gas cavity, set alight to burn off the gas.
A brass vessel was found in rock in 1852 and dated to the deep past. It is a nineteenth-century ornament, and the 'rock' is a conglomerate that formed around it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A theory about the player character's identity in a game's mythology. It is an interpretation of a fiction.
Stone discs with spiral grooves, said to have been found in a Chinese cave with the remains of a dwarf people, and said to record an alien crash. No museum has them and no archaeologist saw them.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claimed secret underground facility beneath New Mexico, housing aliens and joint projects. The claims rest on one man's testimony.
A game blamed for suicides and Satanism. The evidence was never there, and the panic is documented.
A theory that the Dursleys' cruelty is explained by Harry being a Horcrux. The books give the Horcrux explanation for other effects, and not for this.
The Earth's magnetic field is generated by a dynamo in the core, and it was running more than three billion years ago. How, with a hotter core, is the problem.
A derailment, then a controlled burn of vinyl chloride that sent a plume over the town. Both are documented.
For decades, the Ediacaran fossils were a taxonomic orphanage: too big to be microbes, too weird to be animals. Molecular evidence has now placed some of them, without settling the group.
Every person who has ever lived is you, living every life in turn. It is a short story by the man who wrote The Martian — and the internet turned it into a theory.
A model in which the Big Bang is the collision of two branes in a higher-dimensional space. It replaces inflation with a collision, and the two make different predictions.
“The soul is an electromagnetic pattern; the body is hardware.” It sounds like physics. It is a metaphor wearing a lab coat — and the real measurements are more interesting than the metaphor.
A theory that the drink at the Eleusinian mysteries contained a psychedelic fungus. The rite is documented; the drug is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A surveillance clip said to show something impossible in a lift. The clip exists; the reading does not follow.

A student died in a Los Angeles hotel in 2013, and the elevator footage of her last hours became one of the internet's most analysed videos. The official finding is an accidental drowning; the theories have not stopped.

Moore's law was an observation about economics that became a schedule the industry organised itself around. Its end is not the end of computing; it is the end of a very specific kind of free progress.
The civilisation that taught Rome its rituals, and whose language is still only partly read. Their origin was argued for centuries and settled by DNA.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A remembered game about a farmer with a dark secret, searched for and never found. The likely answer is a memory blend.
The proposal that evolutionary theory needs more than the modern synthesis: development, plasticity, inheritance beyond genes.

A mesa in the Cydonia region looked like a face at Viking resolution. Higher-resolution images, taken twenty-two years later, show a mesa. The interesting part is why the first image looked the way it did.

d.t: The FBI and Martin Luther King
d.s: The FBI wiretapped King, bugged his hotel rooms, and sent him an anonymous letter urging suicide. The campaign is documented in the Bureau's own files.
A drug label change negotiated between a regulator and the company, and the revolving door around it.
A mermaid exhibited by P. T. Barnum was a monkey's torso sewn to a fish's tail. It made money, started a genre, and is still in a museum drawer with the stitching visible.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: In 2012 four physicists showed that a falling observer at a black-hole horizon cannot both see empty space and preserve quantum information. The field has been arguing about which assumption to give up ever since.
Every animal, plant and fungus descends from a cell that swallowed a bacterium and kept it. The swallowing is certain; the swallow-er is not.
Food dropped on the floor picks up bacteria immediately. The rule is a joke that got studied.
Three lighthouse keepers vanished from a Hebridean island in 1900. The lamps were trimmed, the kitchen was abandoned mid-meal, and no bodies were found.
A group in West Virginia reported a tall figure with a red face and a hood after seeing a light in the sky. The most economical explanation is a meteor and an owl.
Two creatures from different traditions, run together on the internet. One is an internet invention; the other belongs to Algonquian peoples.
Homo floresiensis is accepted as a species; where it came from is still argued.

Measured intelligence rose by about three points a decade through the twentieth century, in every country with good data. Then, in several of them, it stopped. Both halves of that sentence are strange.
The theory that the whole game series is a child's dream. It was popular, it was abandoned by the community, and the creator denied it.
Two thousand years of medicine built on four bodily fluids. It was wrong, and it was wrong in a way that made sense.

A single mathematical principle is said to explain perception, action, learning and life itself. Its defenders call it the closest thing neuroscience has to a unifying law; its critics call it unfalsifiable, and both have a point.
A country with high saturated fat and low heart disease. The explanation is still argued.
A night-vision video showed two pale, walking figures with no arms or head. The best explanation is a deer seen from behind, at night, at an odd angle.
Put half ping-pong balls over someone's eyes, play white noise, and within minutes most people start to hallucinate. The effect is real; the parapsychology built on top of it is not.

A monolithic gate at Tiwanaku carries a carved figure holding staffs, surrounded by winged attendants. It is a real monument with a documented iconography, and it has been read as a calendar, a portal and a record of visitors.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A 1983 CIA report describes consciousness as a hologram and out-of-body travel as a change in brainwave frequency. It is a literature review written by one officer, and it is cited as though it were a finding.
A granite monument in Georgia carried ten commandments for a post-apocalyptic age, in eight languages. It was commissioned anonymously, vandalised repeatedly, and destroyed by a bomb in 2022.
A deep-sea animal known from carcasses and beaks for centuries, filmed alive only in 2004.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Devils Tower does look like a stump. It has vertical grain, a flat top and a flared base. It is also made of a rock that trees cannot make.
Lamarck's favourite example is not a Lamarckian one. The neck has seven vertebrae, like yours, and the best explanation is not that giraffes stretched.
The claim that the Great Pyramid was a machine for generating electricity, with the King's Chamber as a resonant cavity. It is an engineering hypothesis with no artefact of any machine in it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Liquids cooled into glass never crystallise, and nobody has a complete theory of why. It is a real, everyday unsolved problem.
German agents staged an attack on a radio station and blamed Poland, as the pretext for invasion. Prisoners were killed and left as 'casualties'.
A network of random number generators, said to deviate from randomness when large numbers of people are emotionally engaged. The statistics do not survive the way the events were chosen.
Every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes. It has been checked to four quintillion and proved for nobody.
The claim that fish forget everything in three seconds. Experiments show learning that lasts months.
People remember where to find information rather than the information itself. The 2011 paper that named it is famous; the replications are mixed, which is the honest state of the finding.
A Gnostic gospel in which Judas is asked to betray Jesus. The manuscript is real, and it was published and then conserved.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that the Holy Grail is not a cup but a bloodline, descending from Jesus, and that a secret society has guarded it. The society was invented in 1956, and its documents were forgeries.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A newspaper story about an ancient citadel in the Grand Canyon, with Egyptian and Tibetan artefacts. It was a hoax.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Human females live decades past childbearing, which is rare among mammals. The proposal is that grandmothers helped feed weaned children, and that this is why menopause exists.
Galaxies across a wide region flow toward something in the direction of Centaurus, and for two decades nobody could see what. The answer turned out to be larger than the thing they were looking for.
The silence has to mean something. Either the hard step is behind us and we are lucky, or it is ahead of us and we are early.
A 1976 Viking image showed a face on Mars. Higher-resolution images showed a mesa. The claim survived the picture, which is the interesting part.
About 2.4 billion years ago the atmosphere filled with oxygen, the planet froze, and most of the life then living died. The evidence is in rocks that record the moment the air changed.

The postwar generation got antibiotics, electrification, cars and mass higher education. Since 1970 the measurable productivity dividend has been much thinner — or the measurement has stopped counting what matters.

Two children with green skin and an unknown language appeared in a Suffolk village in the twelfth century. The story is in two chronicles, and the explanations on offer are all more ordinary than the story.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A weight-loss supplement promoted on television with a study that was retracted and a researcher who was paid.
A secret test released radioactive material over Washington state to see how it would disperse. It was detected 300 km away, and the public was told nothing.
A team submitted deliberately absurd papers to humanities journals; several were accepted. The episode is documented and contested.
A suggestion that the griffin's shape comes from fossil dinosaur skeletons in Central Asia. The fossils are there; the transmission is a guess.
US researchers deliberately infected Guatemalan soldiers, prisoners and psychiatric patients with syphilis to test penicillin. The subjects were not told, and the study was hidden for sixty years.
Gut bacteria talk to the brain, and the brain talks back. The question is how much of the conversation changes disease, and how much is a passenger effect.
A chamber beneath the Sphinx, said to hold the records of Atlantis, predicted by a psychic. Seismic surveys and excavations have found nothing.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The proposal that costly signals are honest precisely because they are costly. It explains a lot and is hard to test.
A shadow in The Wizard of Oz is said to be a Munchkin actor who hanged himself on set. It is a bird, and the story has been checked many times.
An empire mentioned in the Bible, recovered from a Turkish mound with an archive of cuneiform tablets.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A statement about which shapes can be described by equations. It is one of the hardest open problems in mathematics and one of the least explainable.
A desert society built hundreds of kilometres of canals, then abandoned them. The cause is argued.
You are a habitat: trillions of microbes, thousands of species, and a genome many times larger than yours. The holobiont concept treats the human and its microbes as one unit, and it is now standard.
The information in a volume of space can be encoded on its boundary. In one kind of universe, this has been demonstrated. Whether it applies to ours is open.

Hopi tradition describes ancestors sheltering underground with the Ant People during a world's destruction. It is a sacred narrative, and the reading that makes it an account of extraterrestrial rescue is an outsider's.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A family in Kentucky reported a siege by small silver figures after a light in the sky. The case is well documented and the leading explanation is owls.
A faulty accounting system made subpostmasters look like thieves. Hundreds were prosecuted, some went to prison, and the Post Office fought the victims for twenty years.
Measure the expansion of the universe nearby and you get 73. Measure it in the early universe and you get 67. Both teams are careful, both error bars are small, and the gap is now five sigma.
A subterranean chamber in Malta that resonates at a specific frequency. The acoustics are measured; the ritual use is inferred.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Stones carved with dinosaurs and surgery, said to be ancient. The carver admitted making them.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: McDonald's ice cream machines break constantly, and it is a franchise-wide joke. The machines are made by one company, their error codes are proprietary, and the repair rules are the story.
A Bavarian enlightenment society, banned in 1785, has become the supposed secret government of the world. The real organisation lasted nine years and left a paper trail.
A reaction-time test said to measure unconscious bias. It correlates weakly with behaviour and its test-retest reliability is poor, which is a problem for a measure used in training and policy.
The claim that Parkinson's begins with an infection or an environmental trigger that travels to the brain. The pathology spreads in a pattern that fits, and the trigger has not been found.

The solid iron ball at the centre of the planet may rotate slightly differently from the rest of it. The claim rests on subtle differences between earthquake waves recorded decades apart, and the disagreement is about the data as much as the physics.
Every closed curve contains four points forming a square. It is easy to state, proved for smooth curves, and open in general.

The claim that perception is a desktop interface, useful but not true, and that evolution optimises for fitness rather than accuracy. It is a serious argument in the philosophy of perception with an empirical claim that has been contested.
A proposal that the Great Pyramid was built using an internal spiral ramp rather than external ones. The evidence is argued.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A six-tonne iron pillar from the Gupta period that has barely rusted in 1,600 years. It is not a lost technology; it is phosphorus, and a dry climate.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A woman found dead in a Norwegian valley in 1970, with erased labels and multiple passports. She has never been identified.
A winged creature said to haunt the Pine Barrens of New Jersey, with a legend about a thirteenth child and a wave of sightings in 1909.
In 1865 William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines increased Britain's coal consumption, not reduced it. The pattern has been embarrassing energy policy ever since.
A three-step classification of civilisations by energy use, invented for a Soviet radio astronomy paper. It measures nothing we can observe, and it is used constantly as though it did.

A Minnesota farmer found a stone in 1898 claiming a Norse expedition reached the American interior in 1362. Runologists have been unanimous for a century that the inscription is nineteenth-century Swedish.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Grooved stone spheres from a South African mine, three billion years old, were said to be manufactured. They are concretions, and the grooves are where crystals grew.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A sea monster described by Norwegian writers, and a possible reference to the giant squid. The animal is real; the identification is inference.
A vast mortuary complex described by Herodotus and Strabo, of which only fragments survive.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: “Larger globe” is not one theory. It is at least three, with different inventors, different evidence and different fates.

Israeli military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews to bomb Western targets in Egypt, in an attempt to damage relations with the West. The operation was exposed, and the political fallout lasted a decade.
Deepfakes do not need to fool anyone to do damage. Their existence lets the guilty deny real evidence as fake — and the studies find that it works.
The greatest library of the ancient world, and the most over-explained destruction in history. It declined over centuries, and no single fire ended it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: At Lindy's delicatessen in New York, comedians believed a joke that had lasted a week would last another week. Mandelbrot gave the observation a name; Taleb gave it a following.
Tens of thousands of brains operated on with an ice-pick-like instrument. The rise and fall are both documented.
Egypt traded with a land called Punt for a thousand years, and its location has never been fixed. The candidates run from Somalia to Yemen.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A hammer found encased in rock, said to be 400 million years old. The rock is a concretion that formed around a nineteenth-century tool, which is what the tool is.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Runners on a circular track at different constant speeds: each will at some point be far from all the others. It is proved for small numbers of runners and open beyond.
Twenty-four hand-cut caves in China, with no record of who made them or why. The absence of documentation is the puzzle.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A boulder in New Mexico inscribed with the Ten Commandments in Hebrew, said to be ancient. The inscription is modern.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A British explorer vanished looking for a civilisation in the Amazon. The civilisation turned out to be real — but not as a city of stone.
115 English colonists, a word carved on a post, and four centuries of stories about vanishing. The likeliest answer is that they did not vanish at all.
A German prospector is said to have found a fabulously rich gold mine in the Superstition Mountains and died without revealing it. People have died looking, and nothing has been found.
Ten tribes deported by Assyria and never heard from again, and centuries of claims about where they went.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Videos show a ripple crossing the Moon's face. The claim is a hologram or a projection. The explanation is the atmosphere, the camera, and the way a bright edge behaves in a turbulent sky.
A Roman glass cup that looks green in reflected light and red in transmitted light. It does this with gold and silver nanoparticles, which is nanotechnology by accident, fifteen centuries early.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Athletes on the cover of the Madden NFL game are said to be injured the following season. The hit rate is high until you count the seasons that went fine.
A traveller at a Japanese airport whose passport was from a country that does not exist. The story has no source, and it is an urban legend.
An analog horror series about 'alternates' replacing people. The name borrows the Mandela effect, and the fiction is explicit.
A large group of people remember the same wrong thing. It is either evidence of a parallel universe, or the most ordinary fact about human memory there is.
A 1978 book argued that the manna of Exodus was produced by a machine the Israelites carried. The argument is built on a medieval mystical text, and there is no machine in the archaeological record.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Children who waited for a second sweet did better later in life. The correlation replicated weakly, and it is mostly about the family.
Two Chicago television stations were hijacked by a masked figure in 1987. Nobody was ever charged.
Maya astronomers recorded the movements of Venus with an accuracy that took European astronomy centuries to match. The tables survive in the Dresden Codex.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Duncan Black proved in 1948 that majority voting on a single dimension picks the median voter's preference. Downs applied it to parties in 1957. The prediction is convergence, and the last forty years of American politics is the counter-example.
Large animals disappeared from every continent except Africa at the end of the Pleistocene. Climate, humans, or both — and the answer differs by continent.
A claim that water retains the properties of substances diluted out of existence. The experiment failed a supervised test.
Men in dark suits who visit witnesses and warn them to keep quiet. The stories are consistent, old, and unsupported by a single verified case.
A video said to show the missing aircraft disappearing into a portal. The video is a composite.
Thousands of inscribed objects 'found' in Michigan, said to record ancient migrations. They were made and planted.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that the Minotaur myth encodes a memory of the Thera eruption or of Cretan earthquakes. The myth is real; the encoding is a proposal.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A claim that an ancient city was destroyed by an atomic blast. The 'evidence' is a scattered set of bones and a misread verse.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A bird-woman image was said to be contacting children on WhatsApp and instructing them to harm themselves. It was a sculpture, a hoax, and a lesson in how a panic travels.
A worm said to live in the Gobi, capable of spitting venom or electricity. The reports come from travellers, and no specimen has ever been produced.
A claimed secret programme at a decommissioned radar station on Long Island: mind control, time travel, and a boy who conjured a monster. The station is real; the programme exists only in books.
An analog horror series in which American monuments are something other than monuments.
The largest sofa that can be moved round a right-angled corridor. The best known answer has stood since 1992 and is not proved optimal.
Listening to Mozart was said to raise IQ. It raises arousal for about fifteen minutes, and the IQ claim was a press release that outlived the paper.

Hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold. It was reported by a Tanzanian schoolboy in 1963, dismissed by his teacher, and is still argued about by physicists with better equipment and no agreement on what would count as an answer.
d.g: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained

d.s: The proposal that our universe is one of many. It follows from some theories and has no direct test.
For twenty years the muon's magnetic moment looked like the cleanest crack in the Standard Model. Then a different way of doing the hardest part of the calculation closed the gap.
Adventure Time is set a thousand years after a nuclear war, and the show reveals it slowly. The backstory is documented in the episodes, not invented by fans.
A worldbuilding project about a national park inside a living organism. It is fiction, presented as an archive of a place that never existed.

d.t: The Nazca Lines as Water Maps
d.s: The lines may mark routes to water rather than sky gods or runways. The puquios — spiral wells — are real, and the lines' relationship to them is argued.

Genesis mentions giants called Nephilim in a handful of verses. The enormous literature built on them — bloodlines, hybrids, modern sightings — is later, and the verses are not a description of a species.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A stone tower in Rhode Island said to be a medieval Norse church. The mortar dates it to the colonial period.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A Japanese internet cryptid: a white, humanoid whale said to live in Antarctic waters. It appears to have been invented online.
A Roman legion stationed in Britain disappears from the record, and has been sent to Scotland, annihilated, or transferred. The evidence points to the dull answer.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The joke-theory that most people are non-player characters with no inner life. It began as a meme, and a survey found a surprising number of people willing to say they doubted others' consciousness.
The colossal stone heads of the Olmec show faces with broad noses and full lips, and have been said to depict Africans. They depict Olmec rulers, and the stone came from local quarries.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Pierre Teilhard de Chardin imagined evolution converging on a collective consciousness he called the Omega Point. Frank Tipler gave it an equation — and the equation needs a universe that is not going to collapse.
Life began once, four billion years ago, and left no fossils. Every account of how is an inference from chemistry — which is why several can be true at once, in sequence.
The claim that the three pyramids at Giza are laid out to match the belt of Orion. The pattern is approximate, the dates do not line up, and the layout has a simpler explanation.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The range of policies a public will accept, and how it shifts. It is a description, not a conspiracy.
A Masonic lodge in Italy recruited generals, ministers and intelligence chiefs, and was exposed in 1981. Its members were involved in the decade's political violence.
A theory about the fate of a ruler in a game. It is an interpretation of a fiction.
Eleven and a half million files from one law firm. The scandal was not that everyone was breaking the law — it was how much of the world's wealth was routed where nobody could see it.
An AI told to make paperclips, and nothing else, would turn the planet into paperclips. It is a thought experiment about goal specification, and it is quoted as though it were a prediction.
A cone-shaped mound in the Siberian forest, with a ring of smaller mounds around it. It has been attributed to a meteorite, a gas explosion and a volcano.
The claim that safety features cause people to take more risks, cancelling out the benefit. The mechanism is real; the size of the effect is disputed.
A defence department programme to investigate unidentified objects, disclosed in 2017 and later renamed and expanded.
The claim that people rise to their level of incompetence. It is a joke with a testable prediction, and the tests have been mixed.
Chemical companies knew about the health effects of persistent compounds decades before regulators acted. The documents are public.
A fired clay disc with 241 stamped signs in a spiral. It is genuinely undeciphered, and it is genuinely not evidence of Atlantis, aliens or a lost Atlantic script.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Recordings said to capture dying Soviet cosmonauts. The recordings exist; the interpretation has never been verified.

A destroyer escort is said to have vanished from a Philadelphia shipyard in 1943 and reappeared in Norfolk. The story comes from letters written by one man in 1955, and the ship's own deck logs contradict it.
A boulder casting a long shadow on the Martian moon was described by a former astronaut as a 'monolith'. It is a boulder, about 85 metres across, on a moon covered in boulders.
A bird that dies and is reborn from its ashes. The motif is ancient; the bird is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The painted people of northern Scotland, known from carved stones and a king-list, whose language left almost nothing.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A 1513 Ottoman map of the Atlantic is genuinely remarkable. The claim that it shows an ice-free Antarctica surveyed by an unknown civilisation rests on a misreading of one coastline.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Every Pixar film is one timeline: animals gain intelligence, humans leave for the machines, and Boo grows up to be the witch in Brave . It is the most elaborate act of fan reading ever assembled — and it never claims to be evidence.
The placebo effect is real, modest, and much narrower than either its critics or its enthusiasts claim. It works best on symptoms you have to report and worst on outcomes a machine measures.
The theory that Ash is in a coma and the series is his dream. It has no support in the show and it can be applied to anything.
A single line about a war, and a theory that Kanto was devastated by one. The line exists; the war does not.
Several people associated with the Poltergeist films died young, and the deaths are said to be a curse. The list is selected, and the films used real skeletons.
An endless complex of tiled pools and corridors, invented on an imageboard. It is a liminal-space fiction, and it is labelled as one.
Two boys disappeared in the Tower of London in 1483, and their uncle took the throne. Bones found in 1674 were never conclusively identified.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Two ways of measuring the proton gave different answers for years. The discrepancy has largely closed, and the episode is instructive.
A claim that the Great Pyramid was a hydraulic machine. The chambers and shafts are real; the machinery is not.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: The Quantum Biology of the Bird Compass
d.s: Migratory birds navigate using the Earth's magnetic field, and the leading explanation involves quantum entanglement in a protein in the retina. It is one of the best-supported examples of quantum biology.
Small gold figurines from Colombia have triangular wings and a vertical tail. Replicas have been flown as gliders, which is the argument, and the argument is backwards.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: French intelligence officers sank a Greenpeace ship in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer. France initially denied it, then admitted it.
Match officials have bet on games and, in some cases, influenced them. The cases are documented in court and league records.
Large numbers of published findings in psychology and medicine failed to replicate. The failure is documented, and so are its causes.
Saudi Arabia and Nigeria both sit on enormous oil reserves. One has a GDP per head around twenty times the other. The difference is not geology.
One vertical line in the complex plane decides how evenly the primes are spread. Ten trillion zeros agree. Nobody can prove it, and nobody serious thinks it is false.
Two groups of boys at a summer camp were set against each other. The conflict and the reconciliation are both documented.
Healthy people admitted to psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed. The study reshaped psychiatry and its data have been questioned.
A shrine in Srinagar said to be a prophet's tomb. The identification is modern, and the site's own tradition is different.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A creepypasta about a Soviet experiment that kept prisoners awake for fifteen days. It is written as a report and it is entirely invented.
Rocks on a dry lake bed leave long tracks, apparently moving on their own. The explanation — ice sheets pushed by light wind — was confirmed with GPS and time-lapse in 2014.
A wooden bird from an Egyptian tomb, about 2,200 years old, was said to be a model glider. It has no tail fin, no airfoil, and no evidence of ever having flown.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that everyone carries a hidden savant inside, unlocked by injury or effort. Acquired savant syndrome is real; the reservoir is an inference with nothing behind it.
A 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin. The argument since has been about what that means for the drugs, and the drugs still work.
Spanish explorers were told of seven golden cities to the north. Coronado found pueblos of stone and mud, and no gold.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The proposal that life with a different biochemistry exists on Earth, undetected because our methods assume ours. It is a serious hypothesis with one famous failed test.

d.t: The Shroud as a Radiation Flash
d.s: The Shroud of Turin is a fourteenth-century linen cloth. The claim that its image was burned in by a burst of radiation at the resurrection explains the image and contradicts the dating, which is the wrong way round.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.t: The Silence of the Indus Script
d.s: A script on thousands of seals from a major civilisation, and no bilingual text to unlock it.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: A theory that the view outside the silo is a screen. It is an interpretation of a television series.
If an industrial civilisation lived on Earth 60 million years ago, would we know? Two astrophysicists asked the question properly — and the answer says more about us than about them.

One crease across the palm instead of two is a real anatomical variant, more common in some conditions. The claim that it reveals character, destiny or 'simian' ancestry is where it stops being anatomy.
The show has run for more than 750 episodes of jokes about the future. People remember the ones that landed. Here is the whole list, checked episode by episode, with the ones that did not land.
The Simpsons appears to predict events. With nearly 800 episodes over 35 years, some of them will match, and the ones that do are the ones that get posted.
Bostrom's argument is not “we are probably simulated”. It is a trilemma, and one of the three horns is boring. The internet took the exciting horn and dropped the rest.

The claim that machine intelligence will improve itself in a runaway loop, and that the curve becomes vertical at some point. It rests on an argument about recursive self-improvement that has never been demonstrated.
A creepypasta about a man in a suit who dances in the street at night. It is fiction, and it is one of the genre's best-known short pieces.
A physicist submitted a deliberately absurd paper to a cultural-studies journal, and it was published.
A man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948, with a scrap of Persian poetry and an unbreakable code. He was identified by DNA in 2022.

The claim that a birth certificate creates a corporate 'strawman' separate from the real person, and that a living soul can escape law by naming it. Courts have rejected it in every jurisdiction that has heard it.

Tsiolkovsky proposed it in 1895 after seeing the Eiffel Tower. Arthur C. Clarke made it famous in 1979. It remains the cheapest imaginable way to orbit and the least available, for one reason: the material.
A spear said to have pierced Christ, and a legend that its holder commands the world. The legend is modern.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The internet is fragmenting into national and regional blocs, with different rules, different infrastructure and different content. It is measurable, and the measurement is the interesting part.
The most famous psychology experiment ever run, and the one with the most documented problems.
Matthew mentions a star that led the Magi to Bethlehem. Astronomy has offered conjunctions, comets and supernovae, and none of them fits the text without strain.

Human brains tripled in size because our ancestors ate psilocybin mushrooms, which rewired us into language, art and self-reflection. It is a wonderful story with a real pharmacology and almost no archaeology.
A creepypasta figure who appears in the background of photographs. The story is fiction, and the photographs are props.
An attempt to suppress information draws attention to it. The name comes from a photograph of a house, and the mechanism is now a standard part of online strategy.
Actors associated with Superman are said to suffer misfortune. The list is long because the franchise is long.
A claim that a celebrity has been replaced by a double. It is the oldest rumour in fandom, applied to a new subject.
A small stone head found in Mexico with features said to be Roman. The object is real; its origin is disputed.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The claim that human technology has become a geological layer of the planet, with its own mass and dynamics. The concept is now used in Earth-systems science.
Early telephones were said to damage hearing and cause 'telephone deafness'. The claim did not survive measurement.
The claim that we use a tenth of our brains. Imaging shows activity throughout.
Thousands of life-size soldiers buried with the First Emperor, individually modelled and painted, found by farmers digging a well.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: Play Tetris for hours and the falling blocks follow you into sleep and into the shower. The effect is real, it has a name, and it turned out to be a window on how memory consolidates.
The claim that cafés, bars, parks and barbers are the places where community actually forms, and that they are disappearing. The concept is well formed; the decline is harder to measure.
A figure in a window in Three Men and a Baby was said to be a dead boy. It is a cardboard cutout of one of the actors.
Thucydides said the war between Athens and Sparta came from 'the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta'. Allison turned that sentence into a dataset.
A Navy pilot filmed an object off San Diego in 2004 that looked like a tic tac and appeared to move impossibly. It is the best-documented modern UAP case, and it is still unexplained.
A claim that the Titanic was swapped with its sister ship for the insurance. The ships' records settle it.
A supereruption in Sumatra and a theory that it nearly ended humanity. The eruption is documented; the bottleneck is contested.
d.g: The ancient world, myth and archaeology

d.s: The diagram showing sweetness at the tip and bitterness at the back. It came from a mistranslation and it is wrong.

d.t: The Trojan Horse as a Ram
